abstract.t: This document defines a YANG data model for a network-wide inventory of physical and logical interfaces, organized by network element. The model provides interface attributes, operational state, and layering relationships, with correlations to network inventory and topology data.

note.t: The latest revision of this draft can be found at . Status information for this document may be found at .

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Network operators and management systems need a consistent inventory of physical and logical interfaces across network elements. Such an inventory supports per-device retrieval of interface attributes and state, as well as correlation with network inventory and topology.
An SDN controller can expose this inventory to northbound clients, such as higher-level controllers and automation systems, to support network-wide operations.

RFC 8343 defines interface data, including operational state and interface-layering relationships, for a server. The IVY network inventory model describes network elements and their components, while RFC 8345 and the IVY inventory topology model describe topology and its relationship to inventory. These models provide complementary information.

This document defines a network-wide interface inventory organized by network element. It reuses RFC 8343 interface data and provides correlations to network inventory and topology. Sections 5 and 6 describe the data model, Section 7 describes the RESTCONF operations, and Appendix A provides a worked example. Discovery and reconciliation of the underlying data are implementation-specific.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
Tree diagrams used in this document follow the notation defined in .

The terms "network element" (NE), "component", and "port" are used as defined in . The terms "network", "node", "termination point" (TP), and "supporting-node"/"supporting- termination-point" are used as defined in .

section.name: Problem Statement
section.t: A network management system may collect interface data from multiple network elements and expose it to clients. RFC 8343 provides an interface model for a server, including interface state and layering. The IVY inventory model identifies network elements and components, while RFC 8345 and the IVY inventory topology model describe topology and its relationship to inventory.

These models do not themselves define the combined inventory view proposed here: interface data organized by IVY network-element identity, with correlations from each interface to its associated inventory component and topology termination points. A client using the separate data sets may need to obtain and correlate information from device, inventory, and topology views, including multiple topology layers.

For example, a controller can learn from the RFC 8345 topology model which link connects two network devices. If that link is realized as a link aggregation group (LAG) and the link degrades (for example, due to loss/errors on one member), troubleshooting typically requires identifying the member interfaces of the LAG on each device. A controller may already collect the LAG and member-interface relationships while building its topology view, but RFC 8345 does not provide a device-scoped interface inventory with operational state and layering that can be retrieved and correlated directly to the topology termination points. This document's model allows the controller to expose that per-device interface inventory and its correlations northbound, so clients can navigate from a topology link to the underlying per-device member interfaces and their state.
The proposed model provides a common structure for that view. Its completeness and accuracy depend on the data available to the server and on the server's discovery and reconciliation mechanisms.

section.name: Relationship to Existing Work
section.t: RFC 8343 Section 3.3 ("Interface Layering") already defines the generic mechanism this document needs: two read-only leaf-lists, "higher-layer-if" and "lower-layer-if", present on every "/interfaces/interface" entry, explicitly described as the YANG equivalent of the IF-MIB "ifStackTable" (RFC 8343 Section 4) . A LAG's members populate the LAG's "lower-layer-if"; each member's "higher-layer-if" points back at the LAG. A VLAN sub-interface's "lower-layer-if" points at its parent physical interface. This document does not redefine LAG or VLAN semantics; it relies entirely on RFC 8343 Section 3.3 for interface stacking .

RFC 8528 ("YANG Schema Mount") defines a mechanism for attaching a schema tree at a mount point. Its Appendix A illustrates device/LNE-scoped mounted data, but the RFC does not prescribe a device key or require one mount per device. This proposal chooses that organization as a data-model design. It uses separate parent and mounted modules. RFC 8528 confines paths in a mounted schema to the mount jail; therefore the mounted augmentation represents cross-model inventory/topology identifiers as strings rather than leafrefs into parent-schema data. A server may use shared-schema parent-reference metadata for XPath evaluation, but this proposal does not require it. This document does not change RFC 8345 , RFC 8346 , RFC 8944 , or the IVY drafts.

section.name: Design Summary

li.t: "network-interface-inventory/device" is keyed by "ne-ref", a leafref into the IVY "network-element" list -- the same device identifier already used by inventory, so no new device identity scheme is introduced.

Each "device" list entry is an RFC 8528 mount point labeled "interfaces-root", under which the server exposes a mounted "ietf-interfaces:interfaces" subtree. The server advertises the mounted module set in schema-mount/YANG Library data.
Every "if:interface" entry in that mounted subtree is augmented (Section 6) with:
an "inventory-ref" carrying the IVY port component identifier, when one is known, within the network element identified by the enclosing device's "ne-ref"; and
zero or more "topology-ref" entries carrying string identifiers for the RFC 8345 network/node/termination-point views corresponding to the interface; and
a "vlan-id" convenience leaf populated from the corresponding RFC 8944 -style topology attributes, so a client does not have to dereference "topology-ref" just to read a VLAN tag.
IP addressing and per-family MTU are represented using RFC 8344 (ietf-ip) within the mounted schema set, rather than being duplicated as additional augmentation leaves.

"higher-layer-if" and "lower-layer-if" are NOT redefined; they are inherited unmodified from RFC 8343 . The server populates this operational view from device/interface data and available LAG/VLAN relationships; the discovery and reconciliation mechanism is implementation-specific.

section.t: The following illustration shows the hierarchy and example correlations. Device identifiers are abbreviated, and RouterX represents another network element. Arrows indicate relationships, not data containment.

section.t: Parent schema module: inventory-network-interfaces

section.name: Augmentation Overview
section.t: The mounted interface augmentation provides three categories of information:

li.t: Correlation identifiers to connect per-device interface entries to inventory and topology views.
Convenience leaves derived from topology data, so clients do not need to dereference topology termination points to retrieve a VLAN tag.
Additional operational attributes and annotations not defined by the base interface model. Interface capacity is available via RFC 8343 (ietf-interfaces) 'speed' (if:speed).

section.t: Normative definitions for the augmentation are in the YANG modules in Section 6. Examples are in Appendix A. Informative comparisons and mappings are in Appendices B, C, and D.
section.sourcecode: +================+==============================+ | Node(s) | Purpose | +================+==============================+ | inventory-ref | Correlate to inventory port | | topology-ref | Correlate to topology TP(s) | | vlan-id | Convenience VLAN tag | | duplex-mode | Augmented attribute | | direction | Augmented attribute | | service-state | Augmented attribute | | floating | Derived/no-topology flag | | notes | Free-text annotation | +================+==============================+

section.name: YANG Modules
section.t: The modules use YANG 1.1 as defined in RFC 7950 and follow the YANG authoring guidance in RFC 9907 .

The model is split to respect RFC 8528 mount-jail semantics. The parent module is loaded in the management system's parent schema. At each mount point, the server advertises a mounted schema set that includes ietf-interfaces, ietf-ip, and device-interface-attributes. The same mounted module set MAY be shared by all devices when their schemas are identical. The server MUST publish the applicable mount-point schema through RFC 8528 schema-mount data and the YANG Library mechanism (RFC 8525 ).

The mounted augmentation contains no leafref into the parent inventory or topology trees. Its cross-model correlation values are strings: RFC 8528 confines mounted paths to the mount jail unless a server configures shared-schema parent-reference metadata. This proposal does not require parent-reference metadata.

section.name: Parent module: inventory-network-interfaces
Mounted augmentation: device-interface-attributes
RESTCONF Operations
section.t: These examples use the RESTCONF URI form defined by RFC 8040 for a resource beneath a schema-mount point. They assume the parent and mounted schemas described in Section 6 are advertised by the server through schema-mount/YANG Library data. Implementations that do not expose RESTCONF may provide equivalent data through another API.

section.name: Retrieve All Interfaces on a Device
section.t: A client retrieves every interface on a device with a single GET against the mounted interfaces container. URI path key values MUST be percent-encoded when they contain reserved characters:

The response representation is the mounted "ietf-interfaces:interfaces" subtree plus augmentation data. The requested device key supplies the network-element context for any "inventory-ref/port-ref" in that subtree. Appendix A.1 shows a shortened full parent data-tree fixture for context; it is not the literal body of this subtree GET.

section.name: Filtering by Interface Type
section.t: RESTCONF does not define generic server-side predicate filtering on list entries. The base operation in this document returns the interface list; RFC 8040 "fields" and "depth" may be used for payload selection. A future revision MAY specify a YANG action or another explicit filter contract for high-interface-count devices; no such action or filter is defined by this revision.

section.name: Protocol Buffers Encoding for Streaming Clients
section.t: RESTCONF/JSON (RFC 7951 ) is the canonical encoding for this document's data model, but some clients -- in particular gRPC- based telemetry and streaming consumers -- prefer a typed binary wire format. A non-normative Protocol Buffers (proto3) schema, "inventory-network-interfaces.proto", is published alongside this document.

Relationship to gNMI. gNMI (gRPC Network Management Interface, gRPC-based model-agnostic subscribe/get for YANG-modeled data) is an established streaming option for this data model . Clients may subscribe to the mounted ietf-interfaces subtree with gNMI; the service-specific proto is an alternative for clients that want strongly typed messages without gNMI's generic "TypedValue" and path-oriented API. It is optional and does not replace gNMI or the RESTCONF operations in Sections 7.1-7.3.
The proto schema defines:

li.t: "Interface", "Device", and "DeviceInterfaces" messages that represent data from both YANG modules in Section 6. The proto uses snake_case names and includes helper fields such as "type_name" for IANA values outside its finite enum; the proto comments document the mapping. "Ipv4" and "Ipv6" carry the per-family addresses and MTU from RFC 8344 ;
a unary "NetworkInterfaceInventory.GetDeviceInterfaces" RPC, equivalent to the RESTCONF GET in Section 7.1;
a paginated "ListDeviceInterfaces" RPC that returns "ListDeviceInterfacesResponse" with "device" entries plus a "next_page_token", for clients iterating over a very large fleet; and

a server-streaming "StreamDeviceInterfaceEvents" RPC that pushes a "DeviceInterfaceEvent" (create / update / delete / initial snapshot, with a timestamp and optional "changed_fields") per interface event. For DELETE, "interface" carries the last-known pre-delete snapshot; initial synchronization uses the distinct SNAPSHOT event type.

section.t: The protobuf schema is informative. Its field naming and helper enum fields are not a normative wire encoding of YANG; the YANG modules in Section 6 are authoritative if the representations differ. The proto carries the device key once on "Device.ne_ref"; "Interface.inventory_ref" contains only the port component identifier.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The parent device list exposes device identifiers and interface inventory relationships. Implementations MUST apply authorization to both the parent device list and every mounted interface schema. Access control on a parent data node does not by itself establish the same policy for mounted data. Servers MUST configure and test access control for mounted instances in accordance with RFC 8528 and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341 ).

The YANG augmentation modules defined here are operational/read-only (their added nodes are config false). The mounted ietf-interfaces schema itself contains both configuration and operational-state nodes; this document does not claim that the whole mounted schema is config false. A GET-only facade MUST reject write methods unless a separate write contract and authorization policy are specified.

Interface identifiers, topology relationships, and device inventory can be sensitive network information. Implementations SHOULD limit access by user, tenant, and device scope, protect RESTCONF/API transport with TLS, and apply equivalent authorization to streamed events and unary reads.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. The "urn:example" namespaces and "example-" module names are placeholders for this individual draft. If the work is adopted by an IETF working group, final namespaces and module names will be selected and appropriate registrations requested in a later revision.

section.t: The complete source data used to ground Appendix A.1 -- three IOS XR routers, their IVY network-inventory, IVY inventory-topology, RFC 8944 L2 topology, and RFC 8346 -style L3 topology -- plus the full parent data-tree fixture from which the Section 7.1 mounted-subtree response is derived -- are published as a companion file set:

li.t: inventory-network-interfaces@2026-11-25.yang (parent module)
device-interface-attributes@2026-11-25.yang (mounted module)
inventory-network-interfaces.proto (Section 7.4)

section.t: The YANG modules, protobuf schema, source topology payloads, and worked JSON fixture are included in this repository. The JSON fixture is a synthetic example; interface state/MAC/ifIndex values not present in the source topology payloads are illustrative, not live-device observations.
The topology payloads describe the following three-router connectivity. RouterA, RouterB, and RouterC are shorthand for the corresponding *.subdomain1.region3.bt.uk node identifiers in the fixture.

section.name: A.1. Example: LAG, LAG Members, and VLAN Sub-Interfaces
section.t: The following shortened RFC 7951 example shows the full parent data-tree shape using the worked example in this appendix. It is a fixture, not the literal body of the subtree GET in Section 7.1; that GET returns the inner "ietf-interfaces:interfaces" resource representation. The complete three-router fixture is included as "examples/mobilecore-region3/05-network-interface-schema-mount-v4.json" in the repository and uses this revision's parent/mount and augmentation module names.

The topology relationships and documented-prefix IP addresses come from the synthetic source payloads. The payloads do not specify IP prefix lengths; the /31 values below are illustrative for point-to-point links, as described in RFC 3021 . The if-index, MAC address, admin/oper states, duplex, and service-state values are illustrative placeholders, not measurements from a live device. In the RFC 7951 encoding below, phys-address is base64 because ietf-interfaces defines it using the YANG binary type.

Note how "higher-layer-if"/"lower-layer-if" give the LAG<->member and VLAN<->parent relationships directly, in both directions, with no topology-network traversal required; "inventory-ref" and "topology-ref" remain available for clients that still need to correlate back into inventory or topology views. "duplex-mode", "service-state", and "floating" (Appendix B) provide commonly needed attributes that RFC 8343 does not define in its base module. IP addressing and per-family MTU are shown using RFC 8344 (ietf-ip) within the same mounted interface entries.
The "TenGigE0/2/0/1" entry illustrates that "floating" can be "true" (no topology-ref entries) while "inventory-ref" remains populated with the known chassis-port component.

section.name: Appendix B. Comparison Against Commonly Implemented Interface Attributes
section.t: The attributes were compared with commonly implemented IF-MIB-based interface inventories. No specific product or API is referenced.

li.t: RFC 8343 covers interface name, description, type, administrative and operational status, ifIndex, physical address, speed, and link-up/down trap enable.
RFC 8344 provides IP addresses and per-family MTU.
Section 6 adds duplex mode, signal direction, service state, and a flag for interfaces without topology references.

Separate connector/equipment identifiers, connector presence, promiscuous and SPAN/RSPAN flags, internal location indexes, soak timers, supported MTU ranges, shared-risk group IDs, entity-alias mappings, LAG end identifiers, and alias names are deferred. inventory-ref/port-ref identifies a port but does not distinguish it from its connector or associated equipment.

section.name: Interface Layering
section.t: The bidirectional LAG/VLAN stacking design in Section 5.1 is validated by real-world experience in OpenConfig : when openconfig-interfaces alone proved insufficient for LAG membership queries, openconfig-if-aggregate added both directions of the same relationship RFC 8343 Section 3.3 provides generically -- an aggregate interface's "aggregation/state/ member" leaf-list points down at its member interfaces, and each member's "ethernet/config/aggregate-id" leaf points back up at its aggregate -- for the specific case of LAGs. That OpenConfig had to add this reverse pointer explicitly, after the fact and for one interface type, is strong practical evidence that a generic bidirectional stacking mechanism is required at the interface-model layer. This document relies on the RFC 8343 generic mechanism instead of a LAG-specific one so that the same "higher-layer-if"/"lower-layer-if" pair also covers VLAN sub-interfaces and other interface-type stacking without a separate leaf per interface type.

section.name: Attribute Comparisons
section.t: The following comparisons identify related OpenConfig leaves and cases for which no direct counterpart was identified:

li.t: "inventory-ref/port-ref": openconfig-platform-port's "hardware-port" leaf provides a similar per-device binding .
"topology-ref": no stored interface-level topology reference was identified.
"vlan-id": openconfig-vlan defines "/interfaces/interface/subinterfaces/subinterface/vlan/match/ single-tagged/config/vlan-id", with the same range (1-4094) .

IP addressing and per-family MTU are represented using RFC 8344 (ietf-ip) rather than as additional augmentation leaves. OpenConfig models interface IP configuration under openconfig-if-ip, and models interface MTU under openconfig-interfaces .

"duplex-mode": openconfig-if-ethernet defines "/interfaces/interface/ethernet/config/duplex-mode" with FULL and HALF values, and models auto-negotiation separately with "auto-negotiate". This document's "auto" value is a convenience for servers that have not yet resolved a negotiated duplex .
"direction": no single generic leaf was identified. A related concept is the client/line role in an openconfig-terminal-device logical-channel-assignments entry for optical transport .
"service-state": no interface-scoped counterpart was identified.
"floating": no equivalent boolean was identified. An absent openconfig-platform-port "hardware-port" indicates no port binding; it does not establish whether an interface has topology references .
"notes": no counterpart was identified for this unstructured field.

section.name: Appendix D. SNMP MIB Object Mapping (Informative)
section.t: This informative mapping gives related SNMP objects where a close analogue exists. It does not constrain implementations.

li.t: inventory-ref: ENTITY-MIB entAliasMappingTable .
higher-layer-if and lower-layer-if: IF-MIB ifStackTable .
vlan-id: Q-BRIDGE-MIB dot1qVlan objects .
duplex-mode: EtherLike-MIB dot3StatsDuplexStatus .
IP addresses: IP-MIB ipAddressTable .
No close SNMP object was identified for topology-ref, direction, service-state, floating, or notes.

abstract.t: YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration data, state data, Remote Procedure Calls, and notifications for network management protocols. This document describes the syntax and semantics of version 1.1 of the YANG language. YANG version 1.1 is a maintenance release of the YANG language, addressing ambiguities and defects in the original specification. There are a small number of backward incompatibilities from YANG version 1. This document also specifies the YANG mappings to the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF).

front.title: JSON Encoding of Data Modeled with YANG

abstract.t: This document defines encoding rules for representing configuration data, state data, parameters of Remote Procedure Call (RPC) operations or actions, and notifications defined using YANG as JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) text.

This document describes an HTTP-based protocol that provides a programmatic interface for accessing data defined in YANG, using the datastore concepts defined in the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF).

This document captures the current syntax used in YANG module tree diagrams. The purpose of this document is to provide a single location for this definition. This syntax may be updated from time to time based on the evolution of the YANG language.

The standardization of network configuration interfaces for use with the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) or the RESTCONF protocol requires a structured and secure operating environment that promotes human usability and multi-vendor interoperability. There is a need for standard mechanisms to restrict NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol access for particular users to a preconfigured subset of all available NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol operations and content. This document defines such an access control model.
This document obsoletes RFC 6536.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for Interface Management

abstract.t: This document defines a YANG data model for the management of network interfaces. It is expected that interface-type-specific data models augment the generic interfaces data model defined in this document. The data model includes definitions for configuration and system state (status information and counters for the collection of statistics).
The YANG data model in this document conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) defined in RFC 8342.
This document obsoletes RFC 7223.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for IP Management

abstract.t: This document defines a YANG data model for management of IP implementations. The data model includes configuration and system state.
The YANG data model in this document conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture defined in RFC 8342.
This document obsoletes RFC 7277.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for Network Topologies

abstract.t: This document defines an abstract (generic, or base) YANG data model for network/service topologies and inventories. The data model serves as a base model that is augmented with technology-specific details in other, more specific topology and inventory data models.

front.title: Guidelines for Authors and Reviewers of Documents Containing YANG Data Models

abstract.t: This document provides guidelines for authors and reviewers of specifications containing YANG data models, including IANA-maintained YANG modules. Recommendations and procedures are defined, which are intended to increase interoperability and usability of Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) and RESTCONF protocol implementations that utilize YANG modules.
This document obsoletes RFC 8407; it also updates RFC 8126 by providing additional guidelines for writing the IANA considerations for RFCs that specify IANA-maintained YANG modules.

This document describes a YANG library that provides information about the YANG modules, datastores, and datastore schemas used by a network management server. Simple caching mechanisms are provided to allow clients to minimize retrieval of this information. This version of the YANG library supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) by listing all datastores supported by a network management server and the schema that is used by each of these datastores.
This document defines a mechanism that adds the schema trees defined by a set of YANG modules onto a mount point defined in the schema tree in another YANG module.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

This memo discusses the 'interfaces' group of MIB-II, especially the experience gained from the definition of numerous media-specific MIB modules for use in conjunction with the 'interfaces' group for managing various sub-layers beneath the internetwork-layer. It specifies clarifications to, and extensions of, the architectural issues within the MIB-II model of the 'interfaces' group. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links

abstract.t: With ever-increasing pressure to conserve IP address space on the Internet, it makes sense to consider where relatively minor changes can be made to fielded practice to improve numbering efficiency. One such change, proposed by this document, is to halve the amount of address space assigned to point-to-point links (common throughout the Internet infrastructure) by allowing the use of 31-bit subnet masks in a very limited way. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for the Ethernet-like Interface Types

abstract.t: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it defines objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces. This memo obsoletes RFC 2665. It updates that specification by including management information useful for the management of 10 Gigabit per second (Gb/s) Ethernet interfaces.

front.title: Management Information Base for the Internet Protocol (IP)

abstract.t: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes managed objects used for implementations of the Internet Protocol (IP) in an IP version independent manner. This memo obsoletes RFCs 2011, 2465, and 2466. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges with Traffic Classes, Multicast Filtering, and Virtual LAN Extensions

abstract.t: This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. In particular, it defines two MIB modules for managing the capabilities of MAC bridges defined by the IEEE 802.1D-1998 (TM) MAC Bridges and the IEEE 802.1Q-2003 (TM) Virtual LAN (VLAN) standards for bridging between Local Area Network (LAN) segments. One MIB module defines objects for managing the 'Traffic Classes' and 'Enhanced Multicast Filtering' components of IEEE 802.1D-1998 and P802.1t-2001 (TM). The other MIB module defines objects for managing VLANs, as specified in IEEE 802.1Q-2003, P802.1u (TM), and P802.1v (TM).
Provisions are made for support of transparent bridging. Provisions are also made so that these objects apply to bridges connected by subnetworks other than LAN segments.
This memo supplements RFC 4188 and obsoletes RFC 2674. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it describes managed objects used for managing multiple logical and physical entities managed by a single Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) agent. This document specifies version 4 of the Entity MIB. This memo obsoletes version 3 of the Entity MIB module published as RFC 4133.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 3 Topologies

abstract.t: This document defines a YANG data model for Layer 3 network topologies.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for Layer 2 Network Topologies

abstract.t: This document defines a YANG data model for Layer 2 network topologies. In particular, this data model augments the generic network and network topology data models with topology attributes that are specific to Layer 2.

front.title: A YANG Data Model for Network and Network Element Inventory
A YANG Data Model for Network Inventory Topology
